description.en: Understand the LSTM gating mechanism — forget, input, and output gates — and how the cell state enables learning over very long sequences.

story_variants.en:
## LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory

LSTMs solve the vanishing gradient problem by introducing a **cell state** — a highway for information to flow through time — and three **gates** that control what information is kept, written, or read.

### The Three Gates

| Gate | Symbol | Purpose |
|------|--------|----------|
| Forget gate | f_t | Decides what to erase from cell state |
| Input gate | i_t | Decides what new info to write |
| Output gate | o_t | Decides what to read from cell state |

### LSTM Equations

```
f_t = σ(W_f · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)   # forget
i_t = σ(W_i · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i)   # input
C̃_t = tanh(W_C · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_C) # candidate cell
C_t = f_t ⊙ C_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ C̃_t       # update cell
o_t = σ(W_o · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o)   # output
h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(C_t)                  # hidden state
```

Where `σ` is sigmoid and `⊙` is element-wise multiplication.

### Intuitive Understanding

- **Forget gate**: Reading "The cat sat on the mat. The dog..." — forget "cat" when you see "dog".
- **Input gate**: Add the new subject to memory.
- **Output gate**: What aspect of memory is relevant for the next word prediction?

> **Key Concept:** The cell state `C_t` flows with minimal modification through long sequences. The forget gate's sigmoid output is near 1 (keep) or 0 (erase), not squashed to tiny values — so gradients don't vanish.

### GRU: A Simpler Alternative

The **Gated Recurrent Unit** combines forget + input into one update gate and has no separate cell state — fewer parameters, similar performance:

```python
# GRU has 2 gates instead of LSTM's 3
z_t = sigmoid(W_z @ [h_prev, x_t])  # update gate
r_t = sigmoid(W_r @ [h_prev, x_t])  # reset gate
```

explanation.en: Forget gate: decides what to erase from cell state
Input gate: controls new information flow
New cell state: erase old + write new
Hidden state: gated read from cell state

Input gate:  i=[0.2, 0.95, 0.3] (write mostly to dim 1)

import torch

under_the_hood.summary: An LSTM keeps a separate cell state that is updated by addition: a forget gate scales the old memory, an input gate adds new candidate information, and an output gate decides how much of the memory to reveal as the hidden state.

steps.title: Four signals from the same inputs
steps.body: At each step the LSTM looks at h_(t-1) and x_t and computes four vectors: forget gate f, input gate i and output gate o, each squashed by a sigmoid to 0..1, and a candidate g squashed by tanh to -1..1. Gates are soft switches: 0 blocks, 1 lets everything through.

nodes.label: f = sigmoid(...)  keep how much old memory
i = sigmoid(...), g = tanh(...)  what to write

steps.title: Worked: updating the cell
steps.body: With c_(t-1) = 2.0, f = 0.9, i = 0.2, g = 0.5 and o = 0.8: c_t = 0.9 x 2.0 + 0.2 x 0.5 = 1.8 + 0.1 = 1.9. The hidden state is h_t = 0.8 x tanh(1.9) = 0.8 x 0.956 = 0.765. Most of the old memory survived, a little new information was written.

props.caption: One cell update, step by step

steps.title: Why gradients survive
steps.body: Along the cell path, dc_t / dc_(t-1) is just f. If the network learns f close to 1 for information worth keeping, the gradient is multiplied by about 0.9 per step instead of a small tanh-and-weight factor: 0.9^10 = 0.35, compared with 0.001 for the plain RNN with w_h = 0.5.

left.label: Plain RNN
left.code:
gradient x (w_h * tanh') per step
0.5^10 = 0.001 after 10 steps

right.label: LSTM cell path
right.code:
gradient x f per step
0.9^10 = 0.35 after 10 steps

steps.title: Four times the weights
steps.body: Each gate has its own weights on both x_t and h_(t-1), so an LSTM layer has about four times the parameters of a plain RNN. In PyTorch, nn.LSTM(10, 20) has 4 x (20 x 10 + 20 x 20 + 20 + 20) = 2,560 parameters, counting its two bias vectors. It returns output plus a tuple (h_n, c_n).

steps.title: GRU: a lighter variant
steps.body: A GRU merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates, update and reset, instead of three. It has about three quarters of the LSTM's parameters and often performs similarly; LSTMs can be better on tasks needing very long memory.

under_the_hood.takeaway: The LSTM's key idea is additive memory with learned gates: old information is scaled, not repeatedly squashed, so both memories and gradients can last for many steps.
